objects: training population; target population; LD; sample size
assumptions: prediction in non-European populations with larger European than target-population training samples
conclusion: Single-population methods are inadequate for non-European prediction because larger European training sets have mismatched LD patterns or potentially different causal effects.
scope: Author motivation for combining population-specific scores.
span: However, all of these methods are inadequate for polygenic risk prediction in non-European populations, because they consider training data from only a single population. Existing training data sets have much larger sample sizes in European populations, but the use of European training data for polygenic risk prediction in non-European populations reduces prediction accuracy, due to different patterns of linkage disequilibrium (LD) (or potentially due to different causal effects) (International Schizophrenia Consortium et al., 2009; Rosenberg et al., 2010; Scutari, Mackay, & Balding, 2016; Vilhjálmsson et al., 2015).

objects: phenotype y; genotype gi; principal components PC; marginal effect bi
assumptions: continuous or binary phenotype; SNP-by-SNP GWAS
conclusion: SNP effects are estimated by marginal linear regression for continuous traits and an analogous logistic model for binary traits, adjusting for ancestry PCs.
scope: No environmental-noise distribution or Bayesian effect prior is specified in this model paragraph.
span: Polygenic risk scores are constructed using SNP effect sizes estimated from genome-wide association studies, which perform marginal regression of the phenotype of interest on each SNP in turn. Explicitly, for continuous traits, we estimate effect sizes b ^_{i} (where i = 1,…,M indexes genetic markers) using the model y = b0 + bigi + bPCPC + ε, where gi denotes genotypes at marker i, PC denotes one or more principal components used to adjust for ancestry, and ε denotes environmental noise. For binary traits, we use the analogous logistic model logit[P(y=1) ] = b0 + bigi + bPCPC + ε.

objects: estimated effects; target genotypes; predicted score
assumptions: effect estimates obtained from GWAS training samples
conclusion: The single-population PRS sums target genotypes weighted by estimated SNP effects.
span: Given a vector of estimated effect sizes b ^_{i} from a genome-wide association study performed on a set of training samples, the polygenic risk score (International Schizophrenia Consortium et al., 2009) (PRS) for a target individual with genotypes gi is defined as y ^ = ∑_{i = 1}^{M} b_{l} ^ g_{i}.

objects: LD threshold RLD2; P-value threshold PT; SNP subset
assumptions: GWAS effects and association P-values; pairwise LD information
conclusion: Pruning and thresholding drops the less significant SNP in each pair exceeding an LD threshold, then retains SNPs below a P-value threshold.
scope: Thresholds are tunable settings rather than model assumptions.
span: Specifically, this “pruning + thres holding” strategy has two parameters, RLD2 and PT, and proceeds as follows. First, we prune the SNPs based on a pair wise threshold RLD2, removing the less significant SNP in each pair (using PLINK; see Web Resources). Second, we restrict to SNPs with an association P-value below the significance threshold PT.

objects: two population-specific PRS; mixing weights alpha1 and alpha2
assumptions: two scores computed using two distinct training populations
conclusion: The multiethnic PRS is a weighted linear combination of two population-specific PRS.
scope: Defines the combined predictor rather than a joint SNP-effect likelihood.
span: Given a pair of polygenic risk scores computed as above using two distinct training populations, we define the multi-ethnic PRS with mixing weights α1 and α2 as the linear combination of the two PRS with these weights: e.g., for EUR and LAT, we define PRSEUR+LAT = α1PRSEUR + α2PRSLAT.

objects: mixing weights; validation data; adjusted R2; cross-validation
conclusion: Primary analyses estimate mixing weights on validation data and use adjusted R2, while secondary analyses estimate weights through cross-validation.
scope: Author procedures for handling overfitting; no optimality or calibration theorem.
span: We employ two different approaches to avoid overfitting. In our primary analyses, we estimate mixing weights α1 and α2 using validation data and compute adjusted R2 to account for the additional degree of freedom. In our secondary analyses, we estimate mixing weights α1 and α2 using cross-validation (see Assessment of methods below).

objects: absolute prediction accuracy; clinical utility; sample size
conclusion: Absolute prediction accuracy remains insufficient for clinical utility, requiring larger sample sizes.
scope: The larger-sample improvement statement is simulation-based rather than a formal guarantee.
span: First, although we have demonstrated large relative improvements in prediction accuracy, absolute prediction accuracies are currently not large enough to achieve clinical utility, which will require larger sample sizes (Chatterjee et al., 2013; Dudbridge, 2013); our simulations suggest that multi-ethnic polygenic risk scores will continue to produce improvements at larger sample sizes (Fig 1).

objects: summary-based prediction; individual-level training data; jointly fitted markers
conclusion: The approach focuses on prediction without individual-level training data, while BLUP and extensions may improve accuracy by fitting all markers simultaneously.
scope: Prospective comparison, not a demonstrated equivalence or universal dominance result.
span: Second, while our focus here was on prediction without using individual-level training data, when such data is available it may be possible to attain higher prediction accuracy using methods that fit all markers simultaneously, such as Best Linear Unbiased Predictor (BLUP) methods and their extensions (de los Campos et al., 2010; Golan & Rosset, 2014; Maier et al., 2015; Moser et al., 2015; Speed & Balding, 2014; Tucker et al., 2015; Weissbrod et al., 2016; Zhou et al., 2013).

objects: LDpred; GWAS summary statistics; LD reference; admixture LD
assumptions: European accuracy comparison; application to admixed populations
conclusion: The authors describe LDpred as more accurate in Europeans than pruning and thresholding but omit it here because explicit LD modeling in admixed populations is complicated by admixture LD.
scope: Extending LDpred for admixture LD is proposed as future work.
span: Third, our LDpred risk prediction method (Vilhjálmsson et al., 2015), which analyzes summary statistics in conjunction with LD information from a reference panel, is more accurate in European populations than the informed LD-pruning + P-value thresholding approach employed here; we did not employ LDpred due to the complexities of admixture-LD in analyses of admixed populations that explicitly model LD (Bulik-Sullivan et al., 2015), but extending LDpred to handle these complexities could further improve accuracy.

objects: related individuals; local ancestry; X chromosome
assumptions: scope of analyses in this paper
conclusion: The analyses do not address improving prediction with related individuals and omit local ancestry and X-chromosome data.
scope: Authors identify these as directions for improving or extending prediction.
span: Fifth, we have not considered here how to improve prediction accuracy in data sets with related individuals (Tucker et al., 2015). Sixth, we did not incorporate local ancestry, which could potentially improve prediction accuracy in admixed populations (Seldin, Pasaniuc, & Price, 2011). Seventh, we did not incorporate data from the X chromosome, which is likely to harbor additional heritability that could improve prediction accuracy (Tukiainen et al., 2014).

conclusion: Rare-variant prediction is left to future work.
scope: No rare-variant guarantee follows from the common-variant analyses.
span: Finally, we focused our analyses on common variants, but future work may wish to consider rare variants as well.

assumptions: using information from a different population or correlated trait
conclusion: The authors view cross-population prediction as analogous to borrowing information from correlated traits.
scope: Analogy only; no model equivalence is asserted.
span: We note that the effects of differential tagging (or different causal effect sizes) in different populations can potentially be quantified using cross-population genetic correlation (Brown, Ye, Price, & Zaitlen, in press; de Candia et al., 2013; Mancuso et al., 2016), and that leveraging data from a different population to improve predictions is a natural analogue to leveraging data from a correlated trait (Maier et al., 2015).
